CVE-2026-73232.title: ffuf is a fast web fuzzer written in Go. Prior to 2.2.0, ffuf all ...
CVE-2026-73232.description: ffuf is a fast web fuzzer written in Go. Prior to 2.2.0, ffuf allows a malicious target server to cause an out-of-memory denial of service because the response size guard in pkg/runner/simple.go checks only the compressed Content-Length while io.ReadAll reads gzip, brotli, deflate, transparently decompressed, or chunked response bodies without a decompressed-size bound. This issue is fixed in version 2.2.0.

GHSA-wc5c-g52x-g44x.title: ffuf denial of service (OOM) via an unbounded response snapshot when -od or -audit-log is enabled
GHSA-wc5c-g52x-g44x.description: ### Summary A malicious or attacker-controlled target server can drive the ffuf process into memory and disk exhaustion by returning a large HTTP response, when ffuf is run with either of the output features - od <dir> or -audit-log <file>. The response body size cap that bounds resp.Data does not cover the snapshot those features take, so memory scales with a body size the target chooses rather than with the 5 MB MAX_DOWNLOAD_SIZE limit. This is adjacent to, and not fixed by, CVE-2026-73232 / GHSA-jcvh-xf52-2cwm. The io.LimitReader added in #897 bounds the read that produces resp.Data and remains correct. The snapshot path is a second read of the same body, in the same function, that was never bounded, and it is present in every released version including those that predate that fix. ### Details In pkg/runner/simple.go, SimpleRunner.Execute reads the response body twice when an output feature is enabled: ```go // Check if we should download the resource or not size, err := strconv.Atoi(httpresp.Header.Get('Content-Length')) if err == nil { resp.ContentLength = int64(size) if (r.config.IgnoreBody) || (size > MAX_DOWNLOAD_SIZE) { resp.Cancelled = true return resp, nil } } if len(r.config.OutputDirectory) > 0 || len(r.config.AuditLog) > 0 { rawresp, _ := httputil.DumpResponse(httpresp, true) // unbounded resp.Request.Raw = string(rawreq) resp.Raw = string(rawresp) } ... limited := io.LimitReader(bodyReader, int64(MAX_DOWNLOAD_SIZE)+1) // 23 lines later ``` httputil.DumpResponse with body=true calls drainBody, which slurps the entire body into a bytes.Buffer via ReadFrom and has no size limit. It runs before the LimitReader, so the allocati on has already happened by the time the bound is applied. string(rawresp) then copies it again. The numeric guard above cannot prevent this. The entire check, including the size > MAX_DOWNLOAD_SIZE test, is nested inside if err == nil, and strconv.Atoi('') returns an error whenever Cont ent-Length is absent. It is absent in two ordinary cases: 1. Transparent decompression (the default path). ffuf sets no Accept-Encoding header of its own and does not set Transport.DisableCompression, so Go's transport adds Accept-Encoding: gzip, decompresses the response itself, and removes Content-Encoding and Content-Length. The snapshot then reads the expanded stream. 2. Chunked transfer encoding. No Content-Length is sent, so the parse fails and the guard is skipped. The snapshot is not gated on whether the response matched any filter. It runs for every response received. With -audit-log, the captured value is additionally serialised for every response: pkg/e ngine/job.go calls AuditLogger.Write(&resp) pre-match, and pkg/output/audit.go marshals the whole Response struct, whose Raw field carries no json:'-' tag. encoding/json escapes control bytes as \u00XX, so a payload of NUL bytes expands roughly sixfold again on the way to disk. Response headers compound this. They sit outside MAX_DOWNLOAD_SIZE entirely, and ffuf left Transport.MaxResponseHeaderBytes unset, so the net/http default ceiling of 10 MB applied. Headers are r etained per response and copied into resp.Raw, into the scraper's source string, and into the audit record. ### Impact Denial of service against the operator running ffuf, through memory and disk exhaustion. The attacker is the host being scanned; no credentials, no network position and no interaction beyond ffuf sending it a request are required. A target that fingerprints ffuf by User-Agent can serve this only to ffuf and behave normally otherwise. Measured against a local target streaming an 8 MiB body of NUL bytes, gzipped to about 8 KB on the wire, 80 requests at the default -t 40: | run | peak RSS | | --- | --- | | no output flags | 318 MiB | | `-audit-log` | 1451 MiB | | `-od` | 1861 MiB | The same run wrote a 3.84 GiB audit.log. Body size is chosen entirely by the target, so neither figure has a ceiling. Scaling from -t 1 to the default -t 40 is roughly fivefold rather than for tyfold, because Go's garbage collector reclaims between responses; the disk consumption is not reclaimed at all. Consequences are the loss of the running scan and of any results held in memory. On a constrained host such as a CI runner, a container with a memory limit, or a small VM, the process is terminated. Because the failure recurs on every attempt against that target, a server can make itself effectively immune to ffuf-based content discovery. Both trigger flags are ordinary documented options. -od is the standard way to retain responses for later review. ### Affected configurations | version | reachable via | also affected by CVE-2026-73232 | | --- | --- | --- | | 1.5.0 and earlier | `-od` | yes | | 2.0.0, 2.1.0 | `-od` | yes | | 2.2.0, 2.2.1 | `-od` or `-audit-log` | no, that issue is fixed | -audit-log did not exist before 2.2.0. ### Patches Fixed in 2.3.0 via PR #934. The response body is now wrapped in an io.LimitReader capped at MAX_DOWNLOAD_SIZE+1 before the snapshot is taken, so every later reader inherits the bound. The existing decompressed-side LimitR eader is retained rather than replaced: where Content-Encoding survives to the manual decoder, the new bound limits the compressed bytes and the existing one limits what they expand to, and both are required. resp.Raw is discarded when the body proves to be over the cap, so no truncated response is written out looking complete. Transport.MaxResponseHeaderBytes is set to 1 MB. The same change also fixes -ignore-body being silently skipped for chunked responses, which followed from the same misplaced guard. ### Workarounds Run without -od and without -audit-log when scanning untrusted targets. The 5 MB body cap is enforced on the normal path, so a scan with no output feature enabled is not affected. There is no wa y to bound the snapshot through configuration in affected versions. ### References - Incomplete coverage of CVE-2026-73232 / GHSA-jcvh-xf52-2cwm. That advisory's remediation is correct for the read path it describes; this is an adjacent read that predates it. - Fix: https://github.com/ffuf/ffuf/pull/934 ### Credits Reported independently and near-simultaneously by @aradinbar, @jankesec , @geoffrey-diederichs , and @movon-ava .
